chapter.name: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet

questions.q: In an imagined journey, a probe starts at the surface in Kanyakumari, travels in a straight line through the centre of the Earth and comes out on the far side. Of the five layers named in the chapter's figure of Earth, which one does the probe pass through only once?
questions.a: The inner core The path runs crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core, inner core, then outer core, lower mantle, upper mantle and crust again. Only the inner core, at the centre, is crossed once; every other layer is crossed twice.
o: The inner core
The outer core
The lower mantle
The crust at the start

questions.q:
A family in a Meghalaya village builds a house of stone and timber, drinks water from a spring and grows rice in a field.
(a) Of the things the chapter says Earth provides, which are used to build the house, and which one supplies the nutrients for the rice?
(b) The timber and the stone both come from Earth, but in different ways. Explain the difference.
questions.a: (a) Rock (stone) and timber build the house; soil supplies the nutrients for the rice. (b) Stone is taken straight from the rock of the Earth, while timber comes from trees, living things that grew in the soil before they were cut.
s: Stone and timber for the house, soil for the rice's nutrients
Stone is non-living rock taken directly; timber comes from trees that grew in soil

questions.q:
Assertion (A): All the mountains, rivers, forests, animals and people on Earth are found in one very thin layer at the surface of the planet.
Reason (R): Below the crust, Earth has an upper mantle, a lower mantle, an outer core and an inner core.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A is the chapter's point that all life sits in the thin crust. R correctly lists the layers below the crust, but naming those layers does not explain why the life-holding layer is thin or why life is found only there.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
The chapter says that among perhaps billions of planets, Earth is the only one where life, as we know today, exists.
(a) Why is the phrase 'as we know today' important in this sentence?
(b) A student says: 'Since there are billions of planets, Earth cannot really be called unique.' Using the chapter, explain why Earth can still be called unique.
questions.a: (a) It shows that the statement is based on what has been found so far; science stays open, and new evidence (for example from Mars, where no proof of life has been found yet) could change it. (b) Being one of many planets does not make Earth ordinary: out of all those planets, it is the only one where life is known to exist and thrive in all its forms, and that is what makes it unique.
s: 'As we know today' means based on present knowledge, open to change
Earth is unique because it is the only planet known to sustain life, not because it is the only planet

questions.q:
For a science fair in Bhopal, a group makes a model of Earth from a clay ball of radius 16 cm. They use these illustrative figures: Earth's radius is about 6400 km, and they take an illustrative crust thickness of 40 km. They will cover the ball with one outer layer to stand for the crust and paint mountains, forests and rivers on it.
(a) How many kilometres of the real Earth does 1 cm of the model's radius stand for?
(b) How thick should the model's crust layer be, in millimetres?
(c) The teacher offers two coverings: coloured paper about 1 mm thick, or a felt layer 5 mm thick that takes paint far better and can be seen from across the hall. The judges will mark the model mainly on whether it is drawn to scale. Which covering should they use? Justify with your answers to (a) and (b), and say how thick the felt would make the real crust appear.
questions.a: (a) 6400 km / 16 cm = 400 km for every 1 cm. (b) 40 km / 400 km per cm = 0.1 cm = 1 mm. (c) The coloured paper. The model is judged mainly on scale, and the paper is about 1 mm thick, which is the scaled thickness; the felt looks better but is wrong by a factor of five. Felt 5 mm = 0.5 cm would stand for 0.5 x 400 = 200 km, five times the real crust, and would hide the chapter's point that the life-supporting crust is as thin as an apple's skin compared to the whole Earth.
s: 1 cm stands for 400 km
Model crust 1 mm (0.1 cm)
Chooses the paper; felt would stand for 200 km, five times too thick, losing the 'thin skin' idea

questions.q: Which everyday observation best shows the property of gases, recalled in the chapter, that makes 'the air doesn't fly off into space' surprising?
questions.a: The smell of incense lit in one corner soon fills the whole room Gas particles move freely and a gas has no fixed volume, so the scented air spreads to fill all the space it can reach. By the same property, air might be expected to spread off into space.
o: The smell of incense lit in one corner soon fills the whole room
Water poured into a glass takes the shape of the glass but stays inside it
A stone dropped from a roof falls straight down to the ground
Ice in a tumbler slowly melts into water on a warm afternoon

questions.q:
Use two new situations to compare the two features in Table 13.1.
(a) A little scented gas is released in one corner of a closed room, and soon the whole room smells of it. Explain this using what the chapter recalls about gas particles, and then explain why the air around Earth does not spread away into space in the same way. (2)
(b) Asha first stands upright and then lies flat on a mat. In which position must her heart push blood upward to reach her head? Explain using gravity. (2)
(c) Name the one force that appears in your explanations for both (a) and (b). (1)
questions.a: (a) Gas particles move freely and a gas has no fixed volume, so the scented gas spreads to fill the room. Earth's air does not spread off into space because Earth's gravity pulls the gas particles of the atmosphere towards it and holds them. (b) Standing upright: her head is above her heart and gravity pulls blood towards the ground, so the heart must pump blood upward against that pull. Lying flat, the head is level with the heart. (c) Gravity.
s: Gas particles move freely and gas has no fixed volume, so the room fills
Earth's gravity holds the atmosphere's gases
Standing upright
Head above heart; heart pumps against gravity's downward pull
Gravity

questions.q: Take Earth's radius as 6400 km and an illustrative crust thickness of 40 km. If Earth were shrunk to an apple of radius 4 cm, the crust would be ___ mm thick.

Read this line from a student's revision notes: 'Gravity holds us on the ground and pulls on our blood as well, so blood can never reach the head.' Test each half of the line against Table 13.1 and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is correct: gravity holds us on the ground, and it pulls on the blood in our body too. The second half is wrong: Table 13.1 points out that our heart can pump blood up to our head, against that pull. So blood does reach the head.
s: Accepts that gravity holds us and pulls on blood
Rejects 'never reaches the head': the heart pumps blood up against gravity
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
Read the statements about Table 13.1, 'Interesting features of the Earth'.
Statement 1: The table links 'the air we breathe doesn't fly off into space' to the earlier idea that gas particles move freely and a gas has no fixed volume.
Statement 2: Gravity does not act on blood, and that is why the heart is able to pump blood up to the head.
Statement 3: The chapter says Earth gives us rock and timber to build homes, as well as soil that helps grow crops.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is wrong: gravity holds us, blood included, towards the ground; the interesting point is that the heart pumps blood up to the head in spite of that pull.
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A giraffe's head stands far above its heart when it holds its neck up.
(a) Which force, recalled in the chapter from Chapter 5, pulls the giraffe's blood towards the ground?
(b) Using the second feature in Table 13.1 ('we can stand on the ground held by gravity, but our heart can pump blood up to our head'), say what the giraffe's heart must do that a person's heart also does.
questions.a: (a) Gravity. (b) It must pump blood upward to the head against the pull of gravity, just as a person's heart pumps blood up to the head while gravity holds the person on the ground; for the giraffe the head is much higher above the heart.
s: Gravity
Heart pumps blood upward to the head against gravity, as ours does

questions.q:
A science magazine imagines three future headlines. A Class 8 class in Lucknow must decide which of them, if it came true, would change the chapter's sentence that Earth is 'the only one where life, as we know today, exists'.
Headline 1: 'Planet found in another star's habitable zone; liquid water likely; no living thing detected.'
Headline 2: 'Rover proves Mars had lakes long ago; still no sign of life.'
Headline 3: 'Living microbes found and confirmed in soil samples brought back from Mars.'
(a) Explain why Headline 1 would not change the sentence.
(b) Explain why Headline 2 would not change it either.
(c) Which headline would change it, and how should the sentence then be reworded? Explain what this shows about the words 'as we know today'.
questions.a: (a) Liquid water makes a planet a possible home for life, but no life has been found there, so Earth would still be the only planet known to have life. (b) Past lakes show Mars may once have had conditions for simple life, as the chapter already says, but no proof of life is found. (c) Headline 3: it is proof of life on another planet. The sentence would become something like 'Earth and Mars are the only planets known to have life'. 'As we know today' shows the sentence rests on present knowledge, and science stays open to change when new evidence is found.
s: Headline 1: water or a habitable zone is not proof of life
Headline 2: past water is not proof of life
Headline 3 changes it, with a reworded sentence and the meaning of 'as we know today'

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'In the chapter's figure of Earth's layers, the outer core lies directly beneath the upper mantle.'
questions.a: False. Going inward the layers are crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core and inner core. The lower mantle lies between the upper mantle and the outer core.
s: States False
Gives the order and places the lower mantle between them

questions.q: Kavya writes: 'The stone and timber we build our houses with must come from deep inside the Earth, from the mantle.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: Both come from the thin surface layer, where rock lies and trees grow The chapter says Earth provides rock and timber for building, and that mountains, forests and all life are found on the very thin surface layer, the crust.
o: Both come from the thin surface layer, where rock lies and trees grow
Stone comes from the outer core, and timber comes from the upper mantle
Both come from the inner core, the hottest and largest store
Stone comes from the mantle, but timber comes from the atmosphere

questions.q:
Prepare a five-point talk for younger students called 'Why Earth is special', using only Section 13.1 of the chapter. Write one point, with one supporting fact, for each of these headings:
(a) Earth among the planets of the universe (1)
(b) Where life is found on Earth (1)
(c) What lies beneath that layer (1)
(d) A feature of Earth we take for granted, and why it is surprising (1)
(e) What Earth gives us for living and building (1)
questions.a: Sample. (a) Among perhaps billions of planets, Earth is the only one known where life exists and thrives. (b) All life is found in the crust, a layer as thin as an apple's skin compared to the whole Earth. (c) Beneath it lie the upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core and inner core. (d) The air we breathe does not fly off into space, although gas particles move freely and a gas has no fixed volume (or: our heart pumps blood up to our head, although gravity holds us down). (e) Earth gives us air, water, soil for crops, and rock and timber for homes.
s: Earth the only known planet with life, among perhaps billions
Life in the thin crust (apple skin)
Upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core, inner core
A Table 13.1 feature with why it is surprising
Air, water, soil, rock and timber

questions.q: In a quiz in Nagpur, Meera answers: 'Earth is the only planet in the universe that has life, and no other planet could ever have it.' Which correction is closest to what the chapter says?
questions.a: Earth is the only planet known so far to have life, among perhaps billions The chapter says there are perhaps billions of planets and Earth is the only one where life, as we know today, exists. It does not say no other planet could ever have life, and it reports no life found on Mars.
o: Earth is the only planet known so far to have life, among perhaps billions
Earth and Mars are the two planets now known to have living things on them
Earth has life because it is the only planet that goes round the Sun at all
Earth is one of very many planets that are already known to carry life

questions.q: A cartoon in a children's magazine shows a banyan tree whose roots grow down through the crust and the upper mantle and then straight into the outer core to 'drink' from it. Using what the chapter says about where life exists and the order of Earth's layers, show that this picture cannot be right.
questions.a: All life on Earth exists only in the crust, a very thin surface layer. Going inward, the layers are crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core and inner core. So the outer core is three layers below the crust, the cartoon even skips the lower mantle, and roots reaching it would be living far outside the only layer where life exists. The picture cannot be correct.
s: States that all life exists only in the thin crust
Gives the order crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core and notes the lower mantle is skipped
Concludes the roots would be far outside the life-holding layer

questions.q:
(a) Name three things the chapter says Earth provides that you use on an ordinary school day, and say what each is used for.
(b) Using (a), explain the difference between a planet that 'allows' life to exist and one that 'sustains' it.
questions.a: (a) Any three: the air we breathe; the water we drink; soil that helps grow the crops we eat; rock and timber that our school building is made from. (b) A planet that only allows life is one where life could exist; a planet that sustains life keeps supplying what living things need every day, such as air, water and food from soil, so life can go on.
s: Three things Earth provides, each with its use
Sustaining means continuing supply of needs, not just permitting life

questions.q: Scientists describe an imaginary rock in space where a few microbes might survive for a short while, but where there is no air to breathe, no water to drink and no soil to grow food. The chapter says Earth 'not only allows life like us to exist but also sustains it'. What does Earth do that this rock does not?
questions.a: It keeps life going by supplying air, water and soil The chapter lists the air we breathe, the water we drink and the soil that helps grow crops as what Earth provides; that supply is what sustains life, not just letting it exist for a moment.
o: It keeps life going by supplying air, water and soil
It lets life begin, but it cannot keep life going for long
It has a thicker crust, so there is more space for life
It is the planet closest to the Sun, so it is always warm

questions.q: Write an everyday situation from your home or school in which you use three of these four things that the chapter says Earth provides: water to drink, soil for crops, rock for buildings and timber for buildings. Then say which part of the Earth each of your three comes from, and what the three have in common.
questions.a: Sample: In the school garden, a student drinks water from a tap fed by groundwater, digs soil in the vegetable bed and sits on a stone bench. Water: the hydrosphere (groundwater); soil and stone: the solid surface layer of Earth, its crust. In common: all three come from the thin outer part of Earth where life is found; none comes from the deep layers.
s: A situation that clearly uses three of the four listed things
Correct part of Earth named for each
Common point: all come from the thin outer part where life is found

questions.q:
The chapter's table gives Venus's radius as 0.95 times Earth's.
(a) Taking Earth's radius as about 6400 km (an illustrative figure), find Venus's radius.
(b) Venus and Earth are nearly the same size, yet Venus is 450 degrees Celsius and Earth 15 degrees Celsius. Using (a), what can you conclude about size as the reason for Venus's heat?
questions.a: (a) 0.95 x 6400 = 6080 km. (b) The radii differ by only about 320 km, so the two planets are almost the same size. Size cannot explain a difference of 435 degrees Celsius; the chapter's reason is Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere, which traps heat.
s: Venus's radius about 6080 km
Size is nearly equal, so it cannot explain the heat; the carbon dioxide atmosphere does

questions.q: Which order of events describes the greenhouse effect on Earth, as the chapter explains it?
questions.a: Sun warms Earth, Earth gives off radiation, gases absorb it, heat stays The Sun first warms Earth; the warmed Earth gives off radiation; gases like carbon dioxide absorb that radiation, so heat is trapped.
o: Sun warms Earth, Earth gives off radiation, gases absorb it, heat stays
Gases absorb sunlight, Earth gets no radiation, Earth warms up, heat stays
Earth gives off radiation, Sun warms Earth, heat escapes, gases cool Earth
Sun warms the gases, gases warm Earth, Earth absorbs all, no heat escapes

questions.q:
Carbon dioxide is found in the air of both Venus and Earth.
(a) How does the chapter describe the air on Venus?
(b) Using (a), explain why the chapter calls Earth's greenhouse effect mild while Venus becomes the hottest planet.
questions.a: (a) Venus has a thick atmosphere made almost entirely of carbon dioxide. (b) On Venus nearly all the air is a heat-trapping gas and the atmosphere is thick, so heat hardly escapes. Earth's gases like carbon dioxide trap only some of the heat, so the effect is mild and keeps the temperature just right instead of making it extremely hot.
s: Venus: thick atmosphere, almost entirely carbon dioxide
Earth's gases trap only some heat, so its effect is mild compared to Venus

questions.q:
A space club in Guwahati invents three planets that go round a star like the Sun for a poster. All figures are illustrative.
Planet K: closest to the star; no atmosphere; average temperature 190 degrees Celsius.
Planet L: second from the star; thick atmosphere almost entirely of carbon dioxide; 410 degrees Celsius.
Planet M: third from the star; atmosphere with some carbon dioxide; 20 degrees Celsius.
(a) Which planet of our solar system is Planet K most like? Give one reason.
(b) Planet L is farther from the star than K but hotter. Explain how this can happen.
(c) Planet M is coolest of the three. What does its carbon dioxide still do for it?
(d) The club imagines sending a lander. Its instruments stop working above 250 degrees Celsius, and it needs an atmosphere to slow it down as it lands. On which planet can it land? Explain why each of the other two is ruled out.
questions.a: (a) Mercury: it is the closest planet to its star and has no atmosphere. (b) L's carbon dioxide traps the heat L gives off after the star warms it (the greenhouse effect), so heat cannot escape and L becomes hotter than K. (c) It traps some heat, a mild greenhouse effect, keeping M warmer than it would otherwise be, as Earth's gases do for Earth. (d) Planet M. Planet L, at 410 degrees Celsius, is far above the 250 degree limit. Planet K, at 190 degrees Celsius, is cool enough, but it has no atmosphere to slow the lander. Only M (20 degrees Celsius, with an atmosphere) meets both conditions.
s: K is like Mercury: closest, no atmosphere
L's carbon dioxide traps radiated heat (greenhouse effect)
M's carbon dioxide gives a mild greenhouse effect that keeps it warm
Chooses M: L is too hot, K has no atmosphere

questions.q: A space agency wants to send a probe that will land on solid rock and drill into it. The target must be a planet that is farther from the Sun than Earth is. Which planet should it choose?
questions.a: Mars Beyond Earth the planets are Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Only Mars is a small rocky planet; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are large planets made mostly of gases. Venus is rocky but closer to the Sun than Earth.
o: Mars
Venus
Jupiter
Saturn

questions.q: A poster in the school science corner reads: 'The greenhouse effect only does harm. Earth would be better off with no greenhouse effect at all.' Should the poster stay up as it is? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: No, it should be corrected. The chapter says the greenhouse effect plays an important role in maintaining just the right temperature on Earth: gases like carbon dioxide trap some of the heat Earth gives off after the Sun warms it. Without this, Earth would lose heat and become too cold for water to stay liquid. What makes Venus too hot is a far stronger effect from a thick, almost all carbon dioxide atmosphere, not the effect itself.
s: Verdict: disagree
Earth's greenhouse effect keeps the temperature just right; without it Earth would be too cold
Distinguishes Earth's mild effect from Venus's strong one

questions.q:
Match each planet with the clue that fits it.
Column A: 1. Mercury  2. Venus  3. Jupiter  4. Earth
Column B:
(a) Its average temperature is about 30 times Earth's, though it is the second planet from the Sun.
(b) Closest to the Sun, yet cooler than its neighbour, with no air to trap heat.
(c) Fifth from the Sun; large and made mostly of gases.
(d) Third from the Sun; its gases absorb the heat it gives off, keeping the temperature mild.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. Venus at 450 degrees Celsius is 30 times Earth's 15 degrees Celsius; Mercury has no atmosphere; Jupiter is the fifth planet and a gas planet; Earth's mild greenhouse effect keeps its temperature right.

questions.q:
Compare the greenhouse effect on Earth with a glass greenhouse used to grow plants in a cool climate.
(a) For each, say what does the trapping of heat. (2)
(b) For each, say what is being trapped or absorbed. (2)
(c) A greenhouse with one broken glass pane loses much of its warmth, while Earth has no walls at all yet stays warm. Using (a) and (b), explain the difference. (1)
questions.a: (a) On Earth, gases like carbon dioxide in the atmosphere do the trapping. In a plant greenhouse, the closed space with glass walls does it. (b) On Earth, the gases absorb the radiation given off by Earth after the Sun warms it. In a plant greenhouse, the warmed air is simply kept from escaping. (c) A plant greenhouse keeps warm only because it is a closed space; once a pane breaks, the warmed air escapes. Earth does not need walls, because its gases absorb the radiation Earth gives off, so the heat is trapped without any enclosure.
s: Earth: gases such as carbon dioxide do the trapping
Plant greenhouse: the closed glass space does it
Earth: gases absorb radiation given off by Earth after it is warmed
Plant greenhouse: warmed air is kept from escaping
Broken pane lets warmed air out; Earth's gases absorb radiation, so no walls are needed

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'The heat that carbon dioxide traps on Earth is heat that Earth itself gives off after it has been warmed by the Sun.'
questions.a: True. The Sun warms the Earth; the warmed Earth gives off radiation, and gases like carbon dioxide in the atmosphere absorb this radiation, trapping the heat.
s: States True
Sun warms Earth, Earth gives off radiation, carbon dioxide absorbs it

questions.q: According to the chapter, which change would make Earth's greenhouse effect stronger than it is now?
questions.a: More carbon dioxide and methane from burning fossil fuels Greenhouse gases released by burning coal and oil trap even more heat in the atmosphere. Earth's mild greenhouse effect would become stronger.
o: More carbon dioxide and methane from burning fossil fuels
More glass greenhouses built by farmers in cool, hilly places
More oxygen in the air being turned into ozone high above
Earth moving into a more circular orbit around the Sun

questions.q:
A science club in Pune pins up this data for three planets, listed in order of distance from the Sun.
Mercury: average temperature 170 degrees Celsius; no atmosphere.
Venus: average temperature 450 degrees Celsius; radius 0.95 times Earth's; has an atmosphere.
Earth: average temperature 15 degrees Celsius; radius taken as 1; has an atmosphere.
(a) By how many degrees Celsius is Venus hotter than Mercury?
(b) Which of the three planets breaks the pattern 'closer to the Sun means hotter', and what does the chapter say causes it?
(c) A member says: 'Mercury has no atmosphere, so nothing traps heat there. It must be the coldest of these three.' Is she right? Judge her statement using the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 450 - 170 = 280 degrees Celsius. (b) Venus. It is farther from the Sun than Mercury but hotter, because its air is almost entirely carbon dioxide, which does not let heat escape: the greenhouse effect. (c) No. Mercury (170 degrees Celsius) is far hotter than Earth (15 degrees Celsius). Having no atmosphere means Mercury has no greenhouse effect, which is why Venus beats it, but Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, from which all planets get their energy, so it is still very hot.
s: 280 degrees Celsius
Venus, because its carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat (greenhouse effect)
Rejects the claim: Mercury 170 is hotter than Earth 15, because closeness to the Sun still heats it though no atmosphere traps heat

questions.q:
Read the statements about the planets of the solar system.
Statement 1: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are small rocky planets far from the Sun.
Statement 2: The four planets nearest the Sun are all relatively small and rocky.
Statement 3: Mars is the planet whose orbit lies between those of Venus and Earth.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only. Statement 1 is wrong because those four are large planets made mostly of gases. Statement 3 is wrong because the order is Venus, Earth, Mars: Earth lies between Venus and Mars.
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
Rohit says: 'Jupiter is the biggest planet, so it must also be one of the hottest.'
(a) From where does the chapter say every planet gets its energy?
(b) Using (a) and Jupiter's place in the order of planets, what would the chapter's general pattern predict about Jupiter's temperature compared with the rocky planets?
questions.a: (a) From the Sun. (b) Jupiter is the fifth planet, farther from the Sun than Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, so by the general pattern it should be colder than the rocky planets. Being large does not make a planet hotter in this pattern; distance from the Sun does.
s: All planets get their energy from the Sun
Jupiter is farther than the four rocky planets, so it is predicted to be colder

questions.q: A farmer near Shimla grows tomatoes in a glass greenhouse because the climate is cool. On a sunny day the air inside warms up and stays warm. According to the chapter, why does the air inside stay warm?
questions.a: The closed glass space keeps the warmed air in The chapter says a plant greenhouse traps warmed air simply because it is a closed space. Gases absorbing radiation is how the greenhouse effect works on a planet, not in a glass house.
o: The closed glass space keeps the warmed air in
Carbon dioxide inside absorbs the radiation from the soil
The glass walls produce heat of their own in sunlight
The plants give off heat as they make their food

questions.q:
A farmer in Leh, where winters are very cold, wants to grow spinach through the winter and plans a glass greenhouse.
(a) Using the chapter, explain how a greenhouse for plants keeps its inside warm. (2)
(b) The chapter says such a greenhouse 'heats up during the day'. Why should the farmer keep the doors shut on a sunny afternoon? (1)
(c) The farmer's son says: 'Our greenhouse warms up the same way Earth does, by gases absorbing radiation.' Correct him. (1)
(d) Give one way the farmer's greenhouse and Earth's greenhouse effect are alike. (1)
questions.a: (a) It is a closed space, usually with glass walls. It heats up during the day, but the air stays in, so the heat does not escape easily. (b) The warm air inside is kept in only by the closed space; opening the doors lets the warmed air escape. (c) A plant greenhouse traps warmed air simply because it is closed. On Earth, gases like carbon dioxide trap heat by absorbing the radiation Earth gives off after the Sun warms it. (d) Both keep things warm.
s: Closed glass space
Air stays in, so heat does not escape easily
Doors shut so the warmed air does not escape
Correction: closed space traps air vs gases absorbing radiation on Earth
Both keep things warm

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Venus has a higher average temperature than Mercury, although Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Reason (R): The air on Venus is almost entirely carbon dioxide, which does not let the heat escape.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Venus's carbon dioxide traps heat (the greenhouse effect), which is exactly why it is hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: If the rule 'planets farther from the Sun are colder' held for every planet, the planet it would predict to be the coldest of all eight is ___.
questions.a: Neptune

questions.q: A made-up news story says: 'A new large planet made mostly of gases has been found in our solar system, going round the Sun between the orbits of Earth and Mars.' Using the chapter, show that this cannot fit what we know about the solar system.
questions.a: The chapter says our solar system has eight planets, which in order are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, so no planet lies between Earth and Mars. Also, the planets in that inner part, Mercury to Mars, are relatively small and rocky; the large gas planets are only Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, all beyond Mars. So a large gas planet between Earth and Mars does not fit.
s: Eight planets, with Mars directly after Earth: no room for another
Inner planets are small and rocky
Large gas planets lie only beyond Mars, so the story cannot fit

questions.q: Imagine Earth's atmosphere suddenly had no carbon dioxide or other heat-trapping gases, while Earth stayed at the same distance from the Sun. What would the chapter lead you to expect?
questions.a: Earth would become colder than the 'just right' temperature it has now The chapter says gases like carbon dioxide trap heat and help keep just the right temperature on Earth; without them more heat would escape.
o: Earth would become colder than the 'just right' temperature it has now
Earth would become as hot as Venus, because more sunlight would reach it
Nothing would change, since temperature depends only on the distance
Earth would become hotter, because heat could no longer be absorbed

questions.q: Imran claims: 'Going by the chapter's own reasoning, if Venus somehow lost its whole atmosphere, it would no longer be the hottest planet.' Check his claim and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes, his claim follows from the chapter. The chapter says planets closer to the Sun are generally hotter and that Venus is the exception only because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat. Without an atmosphere there would be no greenhouse effect on Venus, so by the general pattern Mercury, which is closer to the Sun, would be expected to be hotter, and Venus would lose its place as the hottest.
s: Verdict: the claim is supported
Venus is hottest only because its atmosphere traps heat
Without it, the closer-is-hotter pattern makes Mercury the expected hotter planet

questions.q:
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
(a) Is Mars one of the rocky planets or one of the gas planets?
(b) Using only the chapter's general pattern for distance and temperature, would you expect Mars to be warmer or colder than Earth? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Rocky: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the small rocky planets. (b) Colder. All planets get their energy from the Sun, and planets farther away are generally colder; Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth.
s: Mars is a small rocky planet
Expected colder because it is farther from the Sun

questions.q:
Astronomers (in an illustrative example) find a star whose habitable zone runs from 90 million km to 180 million km from the star. Four planets go round it in nearly circular orbits:
W at 60 million km; X at 120 million km, about Earth's size; Y at 175 million km, much smaller than Earth with the same density; Z at 250 million km.
(a) Which of the planets lie in the star's habitable zone?
(b) What would the chapter expect to happen to any water on W, and on Z?
(c) Y is near the outer edge of the zone. Which planet of our solar system is in a similar position?
(d) A space agency can study only one planet closely for signs of life. Should it choose X or Y? Justify using the chapter's ideas about distance and size.
questions.a: (a) X (120) and Y (175): both lie between 90 and 180 million km. (b) W is closer than 90 million km, too hot, so its water would evaporate. Z is beyond 180 million km, too cold, so its water would freeze. (c) Mars, which lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone. (d) X. It lies well inside the zone, and being about Earth's size, its gravity can hold an atmosphere. Y is at the edge of the zone and much smaller with the same density, so, as the chapter says of a much smaller Earth with the same density, its gravity would be too weak to hold on to its atmosphere.
s: X and Y lie in the zone
W's water evaporates, Z's freezes
Mars
Chooses X: well inside the zone and big enough to hold an atmosphere; Y is at the edge and small

questions.q: Scientists report that the ozone layer above a region has become thinner. Why should this worry doctors there?
questions.a: More of the Sun's UV rays, which can damage living cells, would reach people The ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun that can damage living cells; a thinner layer lets more through.
o: More of the Sun's UV rays, which can damage living cells, would reach people
There would be less oxygen to breathe, since all of it is stored in the ozone
Earth's gravity would weaken there and the air would start to float away
The magnetic field would stop working there and compasses would point wrongly

questions.q: On Earth, a bar magnet hung freely from a thread always comes to rest pointing the same way. Imagine doing the same on a planet that has no magnetic field at all. What would the chapter lead you to predict?
questions.a: It would not settle in any one fixed direction The chapter says a freely suspended magnet settles in a fixed direction because Earth behaves like a giant magnet. With no planetary magnetic field there is nothing to line it up.
o: It would not settle in any one fixed direction
It would point towards the Sun every time
It would settle in the same direction as on Earth
It would spin faster and faster without stopping

questions.q:
A science-fiction story moves Earth to a new orbit far beyond the Sun's habitable zone, in the 'too cold' region.
(a) What would happen to Earth's water there?
(b) A character in the story says some microbes might still survive, but crops, animals and people would not. Is this consistent with the chapter? Explain.
questions.a: (a) All the water would freeze. (b) Yes. The chapter says some microbes, like certain bacteria, can survive in frozen environments, but in such extreme conditions it would be impossible for most life forms, especially plants, animals and humans, to grow and thrive.
s: All the water would freeze
Consistent: some bacteria survive frozen conditions, but most life (plants, animals, humans) could not thrive

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'Earth's magnetic field only makes a compass needle point in a fixed direction; it does nothing to protect life.'
questions.a: False. Earth's magnetic field acts like a protective shield: it pushes many harmful high-energy particles (cosmic rays and the solar wind) away from Earth. These particles could damage the atmosphere and reduce the ozone layer, so the field keeps the atmosphere, and hence life, safe.
s: States False
The field pushes away cosmic rays and solar wind that would damage the atmosphere and ozone layer

questions.q:
Earth's magnetic field, its atmosphere and its ozone layer work together to keep living cells safe.
(a) Name the two kinds of high-energy particles that hit Earth and say where each comes from. (1)
(b) Describe what the magnetic field does to these particles. (1)
(c) Explain why the ozone layer depends on both the atmosphere and the magnetic field. (2)
(d) Using (a) to (c), explain in one sentence why the chapter says the magnetic field keeps 'life on our planet safe'. (1)
questions.a: (a) Cosmic rays, from far across the universe, and the solar wind, from the Sun. (b) It acts like a shield and pushes many of these particles away from Earth. (c) The ozone layer forms from oxygen in the atmosphere, so it needs the atmosphere (held by Earth's gravity) to exist; and the particles can damage the atmosphere and reduce the ozone layer, so it needs the magnetic field to push them away. (d) By keeping the particles away, the field protects the atmosphere and its ozone layer, which blocks the UV rays that damage living cells.
s: Cosmic rays from across the universe, solar wind from the Sun
The field pushes many particles away
Ozone forms from atmospheric oxygen, so it needs the atmosphere
Particles reduce ozone, so it needs the field's protection
Field protects atmosphere and ozone, which block UV harmful to cells

questions.q: Astronomers study two planets of a distant star (an illustrative example). Planet A has a thick atmosphere, but all its water is frozen solid. Planet B has a thin atmosphere and oceans of liquid water. Using the chapter's definition, which planet lies in the star's habitable zone?
questions.a: Planet B, because water stays liquid at its distance The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star (the Sun or another star) over which water remains liquid. Having an atmosphere is not the test.
o: Planet B, because water stays liquid at its distance
Planet A, because it has the thicker atmosphere
Both, because both of them have some water of one kind
Neither, because only the Sun can have such a zone

questions.q: A quiz team writes this answer: 'Earth supports life simply because it is at the right distance from the Sun. Nothing else about Earth matters.' Would you give the answer full marks? Justify with the chapter.
questions.a: No. Distance is the most important reason, because it lets water stay liquid, but the chapter says it is not the only factor. Earth is also the right size: its gravity holds an atmosphere (with oxygen and the ozone layer), yet is not so strong that it would crush living things. Its nearly circular orbit keeps sunlight steady, and its magnetic field pushes away harmful cosmic rays and solar wind.
s: Verdict: disagree, distance is the most important but not the only factor
Size: gravity holds the atmosphere and ozone layer, without crushing life
Any one more: nearly circular orbit, or magnetic field shielding from particles

questions.q:
From space, an astronaut sees Earth as mostly blue, while Mars looks reddish-brown with no blue at all.
(a) What does the blue tell her about Earth's surface, and what name does it give Earth?
(b) Using the chapter's ideas about distance from the Sun, explain why Earth can have so much liquid water today while scientists think Mars may have had it only in the past.
questions.a: (a) Most of Earth's surface is covered with water, which makes it look blue: the Blue Planet. (b) Earth is at just the right distance from the Sun for water to stay liquid. Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone, so conditions for liquid water there are borderline; scientists think it may once have had liquid water, even lakes, but it does not have such oceans now.
s: Mostly covered with water, so the Blue Planet
Earth at the right distance; Mars at the edge of the zone, so borderline

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A freely suspended magnet settles in a fixed direction because Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet.
Statement 2: Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone, and scientists think it may once have had liquid water.
Statement 3: Earth's nearly circular orbit keeps the sunlight and heat it receives nearly steady through the year.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1, 2 and 3. All three are what the chapter says: Earth behaves like a giant magnet; Mars is at the edge of the habitable zone and may once have had liquid water; the nearly circular orbit keeps sunlight and heat nearly steady, preventing extreme summers and winters.
o: Statements 1, 2 and 3
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q:
A satellite detects two streams of tiny, high-energy particles. Stream P arrives from the direction of the Sun. Stream Q arrives from far across the universe.
(a) Name Stream P and Stream Q as the chapter does.
(b) A student says Earth's magnetic field can protect us from only one of these streams. Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) P is the solar wind; Q is cosmic rays. (b) No. The chapter says Earth's magnetic field acts like a protective shield and pushes many of these harmful particles away; it describes this for both the cosmic rays and the solar wind, keeping the atmosphere safe.
s: P solar wind, Q cosmic rays
No: the field pushes away many particles of both kinds

questions.q:
The chapter says Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone.
(a) What does lying at the 'edge' suggest about liquid water on Mars, compared with Earth?
(b) Rovers have explored Mars and found no proof of life. Does this prove that Mars never had any life? Explain.
(c) Using your answers, explain why Mars continues to interest scientists.
questions.a: (a) At the edge, conditions for liquid water are borderline, unlike Earth, which is at just the right distance. (b) No. Finding no proof so far is not proof that life never existed; scientists think Mars may once have had liquid water, maybe lakes, and conditions that could support simple life, and science stays open to new clues. (c) Because Mars is at the edge of the zone and may have had liquid water in the past, it may once have had conditions for simple life, so searching it could tell us whether life ever arose beyond Earth.
s: Edge means borderline conditions for liquid water
No proof found is not proof of no life; Mars may once have had water and science stays open
Mars interests scientists because past water may mean past conditions for simple life

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Seen from space, Earth looks blue.
Reason (R): Earth's ozone layer blocks the blue part of sunlight and sends it back into space.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Earth looks blue because most of its surface is covered with a vast amount of water, which is why it is called the Blue Planet. The ozone layer is described as blocking harmful ultraviolet rays, not blue light.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Justify the statement: 'Earth is just the right size for life.'
(a) What would happen to the atmosphere if Earth were much smaller but had the same average density? Explain the reason, and state what the chapter says about the atmospheres of Mars and Mercury right after making this point. (2)
(b) What does the chapter suggest could happen if Earth were much larger, with much stronger gravity? (1)
(c) Give two reasons, from this chapter, why keeping the atmosphere matters for life. (2)
questions.a: (a) Its gravity would be too weak to hold on to the gases of the atmosphere, and they would escape into space. The chapter then notes that on Mars the atmosphere is 100 times thinner than on Earth, and Mercury has no atmosphere at all. (b) Gravity could pull us down with such force that our bones could be crushed. (c) Any two: the atmosphere contains oxygen, which lets us breathe and is needed by almost all life; some oxygen forms the ozone layer, which blocks harmful UV rays that damage living cells; its gases give a mild greenhouse effect that keeps the temperature right.
s: Weaker gravity cannot hold the gases, which escape into space
States the chapter's note: Mars's atmosphere 100 times thinner, Mercury none
Much larger: much stronger gravity could crush bones
First reason the atmosphere matters (oxygen to breathe, or ozone, or warmth)
Second, different reason

questions.q: An imaginary planet in a star's habitable zone is several times larger than Earth, with much stronger gravity. Which danger to animals like us does the chapter suggest for such a planet?
questions.a: Gravity could pull us down so hard that our bones could be crushed The chapter says that if a planet were too large and gravity much stronger, it would perhaps pull us down with such force that our bones could get crushed.
o: Gravity could pull us down so hard that our bones could be crushed
Its gravity would be too weak, so the gases of its air would escape
It would have no magnetic field, because large planets cannot have one
Its water would all evaporate, because large planets are always hot

questions.q:
Match each observation with the feature of Earth that the chapter says is responsible.
Column A:
1. A compass needle hung freely settles pointing the same way every time.
2. Ultraviolet rays from the Sun are mostly stopped high above the ground.
3. The gases of the air stay around Earth instead of escaping into space.
4. Oceans stay liquid instead of boiling away or freezing solid.
Column B: (a) Earth's size and its gravity  (b) Earth's distance from the Sun  (c) Earth's magnetic field  (d) The ozone layer
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b. Earth behaves like a giant magnet; the ozone layer blocks UV rays; Earth's size gives it enough gravity to hold its atmosphere; its distance from the Sun lets water stay liquid.

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Kolkata compares four imaginary planets. All four go round a Sun-like star inside its habitable zone. The other facts (illustrative) are:
Planet A: nearly circular orbit; Earth's size; an atmosphere with no oxygen in it.
Planet B: very stretched oval orbit; Earth's size; atmosphere with oxygen.
Planet C: nearly circular orbit; much larger than Earth, with much stronger gravity; atmosphere with oxygen.
Planet D: nearly circular orbit; Earth's size; atmosphere with oxygen; a magnetic field.
(a) Planet A has an atmosphere. Why would it still lack the protection Earth's atmosphere gives against the Sun's UV rays?
(b) What problem would Planet B's orbit cause?
(c) What danger does the chapter suggest for living things on Planet C?
(d) The group can send one probe. Which planet should it visit, and what must the probe find there before anyone can say the planet has life?
questions.a: (a) The ozone layer forms from oxygen in the atmosphere; with no oxygen, Planet A has no ozone layer to block harmful UV rays. (b) Sunlight and heat would not stay steady through its year, giving extreme summers and winters. (c) Its much stronger gravity could pull living things down so hard that bones could be crushed. (d) Planet D, which matches Earth on distance, orbit, size, oxygen and magnetic field. But suitable conditions are not proof: the probe must find living things themselves, since even Mars, which may once have had water, has shown no proof of life.
s: No oxygen means no ozone layer, so no UV shield
B: unsteady sunlight, extreme summers and winters
C: much stronger gravity could crush bones
Chooses D and says conditions are not proof; living things must be found

questions.q: Suppose Earth's orbit were stretched into a long oval, bringing it very close to the Sun for part of the year and very far for another part, with the same average distance. What would the chapter lead us to expect?
questions.a: Very hot and very cold spells within one year at most places The chapter says Earth's nearly circular orbit keeps sunlight and heat nearly steady through the year, preventing extreme summers and winters. A stretched orbit would remove that steadiness.
o: Very hot and very cold spells within one year at most places
No change at all, since the average distance would stay the same
Water would stay liquid everywhere through every month of the year
Earth's gravity would become too weak to hold its atmosphere

questions.q:
India's Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission) was launched by ISRO in 2013 and carried tools to look for signs of past water.
(a) Why does it make sense to search for signs of past water on Mars rather than on Mercury?
(b) Explain why 'signs of past water' would help scientists decide whether Mars was ever suitable for life.
questions.a: (a) Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone and may once have had liquid water. Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and has no atmosphere at all, so liquid water is not expected there. (b) From what we know, liquid water is essential for life to evolve; if Mars once had liquid water, it may once have had conditions that could support simple life.
s: Mars at the edge of the habitable zone vs Mercury closest with no atmosphere
Liquid water is essential for life, so past water suggests past conditions for life

questions.q: A scientist writes this conclusion about an imaginary planet: 'So this planet cannot keep a thick atmosphere, even though it lies inside its star's habitable zone.' Write two facts about the planet (label them illustrative) that would lead to this conclusion, and give the chain of reasoning from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample facts: the planet is about one-third of Earth's size, with the same average density as Earth; it lies near the inner edge of its star's habitable zone, so its water could stay liquid. Reasoning: a much smaller planet with the same density has much weaker gravity; gravity is what holds the gases of an atmosphere; with weak gravity the gases escape into space, so the planet cannot keep a thick atmosphere, whatever its distance from the star.
s: Facts that make the planet much smaller with the same density (labelled illustrative)
Smaller with same density means weaker gravity
Weak gravity cannot hold the gases, which escape, whatever the distance

questions.q:
In June, monsoon winds carry moist air from the sea over Kerala, and farmers plant rice soon after the rains begin.
(a) What does the water vapour in this air form, and what does it bring?
(b) Using (a), explain how the atmosphere and the hydrosphere together decide when the farmers can plant.
questions.a: (a) It forms clouds and brings rain. (b) Moving air in the atmosphere carries the water vapour and shapes the rainfall; the rain refills rivers, lakes and groundwater (hydrosphere) and wets the soil, and freshwater is needed to grow crops, so the farmers plant when the rain arrives.
s: Clouds that bring rain
Moving air brings the rain, which refills water and soil; crops need freshwater, so planting follows the rain

questions.q: After a long football match in the Chennai heat, a player sweats, which cools her body, and then drinks two bottles of water. Which roles of water in animals, as named in the chapter, are most directly at work?
questions.a: Regulating body temperature and keeping the body hydrated Sweating that cools the body is water regulating temperature; drinking water restores hydration. Carrying nutrients from soil to leaves happens in plants, and digestion is not what sweating and drinking show here.
o: Regulating body temperature and keeping the body hydrated
Transporting nutrients from the soil, as it does inside plants
Forming clouds over the ground and bringing rain to the field
Aiding the digestion of the meal she ate before the match

questions.q:
A potted tulsi plant on a Delhi balcony stands in soil that is rich in nutrients, but the soil has dried out completely in a hot week, and the leaves droop and turn pale.
(a) The nutrients are in the soil but are not reaching the leaves. Which role of water in plants, named in the chapter, has stopped?
(b) Why does it matter for this role that water is a good solvent?
(c) Which Earth system holds the water that refills the soil in fields and gardens through rain, rivers, lakes and groundwater?
questions.a: (a) Transporting nutrients from the soil to the leaves. (b) Nutrients from the soil dissolve in water, so water can carry them up to the leaves; with no water in the soil, the nutrients stay where they are. (c) The hydrosphere, which is all of Earth's water, including rivers, lakes and groundwater.
s: Transport of nutrients from soil to leaves
Nutrients dissolve in water, which carries them
Hydrosphere

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Soil gets its nutrients only from the remains of plants and animals, and not from rocks.
Statement 2: Geodiversity includes the processes that shape and alter landforms, rocks and soils, not only their variety.
Statement 3: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil by breaking down dead matter.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is wrong because soil nutrients like nitrogen and potassium come from both the slow breakdown of rocks and the remains of plants and animals.
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'Without its atmosphere, Earth could not sustain life.' Give five different roles of the atmosphere from Section 13.4 of the chapter, each with what it does for living things.
questions.a: Any five: (1) It contains oxygen, which humans, animals and plants use for respiration. (2) It supplies the carbon dioxide that plants use, with water and sunlight, to make food by photosynthesis. (3) Its mild greenhouse effect keeps the temperature just high enough for water to stay liquid; without it Earth would lose heat to space and become too cold. (4) Water vapour in the air forms clouds and brings rain or snow, refilling rivers, lakes and groundwater. (5) Moving air shapes weather and rainfall, which influence farming, water supply and life on land.
s: First role with its effect on life
Second role
Third role
Fourth role
Fifth role

questions.q:
Match each item with the Earth system it belongs to.
Column A: 1. Groundwater drawn by a village hand pump  2. Iron ore mined in Odisha  3. The carbon dioxide a mango tree takes in  4. Fungi breaking down fallen leaves
Column B: (a) Atmosphere  (b) Biosphere  (c) Hydrosphere  (d) Geosphere
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b. Groundwater is part of the hydrosphere; ores and minerals are solid parts of the Earth (geosphere); carbon dioxide is in the air (atmosphere); fungi are living decomposers (biosphere).

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'If Earth had no atmosphere at all, it would be colder than it is now, even though it would be just as far from the Sun.'
questions.a: True. Radiation from the Sun heats the Earth, and some of this heat is trapped by the atmosphere through the mild greenhouse effect. Without an atmosphere, the Earth would lose heat to space and become too cold, whatever its distance.
s: States True
Atmosphere traps some heat (mild greenhouse effect); without it heat is lost to space

questions.q: A brochure for a new hill resort says: 'Cutting down this forest to build cottages will affect only the trees. The rain, soil, air and wildlife of the valley will stay exactly as before.' Using the chapter, show that this promise cannot be relied on.
questions.a: The chapter says Earth is a vast living system in which land, air, water and living things support and affect one another. It gives cutting down a forest as its example of a small change in one part that can impact rainfall, soil, air quality and the animals that live there. So removing the forest is not a change to the trees alone, and the brochure's promise goes against what the chapter says.
s: Earth's systems support and affect one another
Cutting a forest is the chapter's own example of a change that spreads
Names the effects on rainfall, soil, air quality and animals, so the promise fails

questions.q: A hill forest in Uttarakhand is cleared to build a road. Which set of effects does the chapter say such a change in one part of Earth's system can have?
questions.a: Changes in rainfall, soil, air quality and the animals living there The chapter uses cutting down a forest as its example of a small change in one part that affects rainfall, soil, air quality and animals.
o: Changes in rainfall, soil, air quality and the animals living there
Changes to the animals only, since land and air are not living things
No real change, since one forest is a tiny part of a very large Earth
Changes to rainfall only, because forests are part of the hydrosphere

questions.q:
A school in Thrissur collects about 15 sacks of dead leaves from its grounds every month. The caretaker burns them in a corner of the field: it takes an hour and needs no space, but the smoke drifts over the classrooms. The eco club suggests a pit at the back of the garden instead. The pit takes up a corner of land, the leaves need about 3 months to be broken down by small organisms, and the pit can smell in the rains; after that, the material is dug into the vegetable beds.
(a) What are the organisms that break down the leaves called, and what do they return to the soil?
(b) If the pit is emptied every 3 months, how many sacks of leaves must it hold at a time?
(c) Weigh the two methods and decide which the school should use. Justify using the chapter's ideas about the linked Earth systems.
questions.a: (a) Decomposers; they break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. (b) 15 x 3 = 45 sacks. (c) The pit. Burning is quicker and needs no land, but its smoke goes into the air the students breathe, and the chapter says air pollution can cause breathing problems. The pit costs space and time and may smell in the rains, but it puts the leaves through the decomposers (biosphere), which return nutrients to the soil (geosphere) of the vegetable beds and keeps the atmosphere clean. A single corner pit for 45 sacks is a small price for that.
s: Decomposers, returning nutrients to the soil
45 sacks
Chooses the pit, weighing burning's speed against smoke and the pit's space and time against nutrient return and clean air

questions.q: A school globe's surface is divided into 200 equal squares. Since water covers about 70 per cent of Earth's surface, about ___ of the squares would show water.

(a) In photosynthesis, which gas do plants take from the air and which gas do they release?
(b) Using (a), explain how photosynthesis links the biosphere with the atmosphere in a way that helps animals.
questions.a: (a) Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen (using water from the soil, in sunlight). (b) Plants (part of the biosphere) take carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and put oxygen back into it; humans and animals use this oxygen from the atmosphere for respiration. So living things and the air keep supplying each other.
s: Takes in carbon dioxide, releases oxygen
Oxygen released into the air is used by animals for respiration, linking life and air

questions.q: To make poor potting soil richer, a gardener mixes in crushed rock dust and rotted leaves and dung. Which idea from the chapter is she copying?
questions.a: Soil nutrients come from broken rock and the remains of living things Nutrients like nitrogen and potassium come from the slow breakdown of rocks and the remains of plants and animals; she is speeding up both sources.
o: Soil nutrients come from broken rock and the remains of living things
Soil gets its nutrients mainly from the carbon dioxide in the open air
Soil nutrients come from rainwater after it falls through clouds
Soil gets its nutrients only from the sunlight that falls on it

questions.q:
A farming village in Vidarbha keeps a record of yearly rainfall and of how far below the ground the water stands in the village well (illustrative figures).
Year 1: rainfall 900 mm; water 6 m below ground.
Year 2: rainfall 700 mm; water 8 m below ground.
Year 3: rainfall 500 mm; water 11 m below ground.
Year 4: rainfall 650 mm; water 9 m below ground.
(a) Which part of the hydrosphere does the well draw on?
(b) Between Year 1 and Year 3, by how many millimetres did rainfall drop, and by how many metres did the water level fall?
(c) What pattern links rainfall and the well, and how does the chapter explain it? Use Year 4 as a check.
(d) The panchayat can afford one project: deepen the well by another 5 m (about Rs 2 lakh), or dig a large pond that collects rainwater and lets it soak into the ground (about Rs 2.5 lakh). Using (c), which project deals with the cause of the problem? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Groundwater. (b) Rainfall dropped by 900 - 500 = 400 mm; the water level fell by 11 - 6 = 5 m. (c) Less rain, deeper water; more rain, shallower water. Rain refills rivers, lakes and underground water, so a wetter year refills the well; in Year 4, rain rose by 150 mm and the water came 2 m closer to the surface, as the pattern predicts. (d) The pond. The data in (c) show the well falls when less rain refills the groundwater. The pond keeps more of each year's rain on the land to soak in and refill the groundwater, so it works on the cause. Deepening the well only reaches water that is still falling; after a few more dry years the deeper well could fail too.
s: Groundwater
400 mm less rain, water 5 m deeper
Less rain gives deeper water because rain refills groundwater; Year 4 fits
Chooses the pond because it refills groundwater, the cause; deepening only follows the falling level

questions.q: Differentiate between the biosphere and the geosphere, giving one example of each. Then say why a fish in a river counts as part of the biosphere, and which Earth system the pebbles themselves (as solid rock) belong to.
questions.a: The biosphere is all living beings together with the places where they live (land, water and air); for example, a tiger in a forest. The geosphere is the solid part of the Earth: rocks, soils and minerals; for example, a granite hill. The fish is a living being, so it is part of the biosphere. The pebbles themselves are solid rock, so they belong to the geosphere.
s: Defines both the biosphere and the geosphere
Gives an example of each; the fish is living so biosphere, the pebbles are solid rock so geosphere

questions.q:
Read the statements about the hydrosphere.
Statement 1: The hydrosphere is home to millions of life forms, from tiny plankton to giant whales, and many are still being discovered.
Statement 2: The hydrosphere includes only the seas and oceans, because the water in rivers and wells is too little to count.
Statement 3: Freshwater is needed to grow crops and support people around the world.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is wrong: the hydrosphere is all of Earth's water, in ponds, lakes, rivers, springs, seas, oceans and groundwater.
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q: Asha claims: 'The coal burnt in a power station and the iron in a bicycle frame come from the same Earth system as the soil in a farmer's field.' Check her claim using the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. The geosphere is the solid part of the Earth, made of rocks, soils and minerals. The chapter says minerals from this layer give us salt, coal, oil and metals like iron and copper, and soil is also part of the geosphere. So coal, iron and farm soil all come from the geosphere.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
The geosphere includes rocks, soils and minerals
Coal and iron come from its minerals, and soil is part of it too

questions.q:
Compare the Thar desert, the Sundarbans delta and the slopes of the Himalaya.
(a) Is the difference in their landforms, rocks and soils an example of biodiversity or of geodiversity, as the chapter uses the terms?
(b) Using (a), explain why this difference matters for living things.
questions.a: (a) Geodiversity: the variety of landforms, rocks and soils, along with the processes that shape them. (b) Geodiversity creates unique habitats where different types of life can thrive, so each of these places supports different living things.
s: Geodiversity
It creates unique habitats where different types of life thrive

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The geosphere includes only the hard rocks deep below the ground, not the soil at the surface.
Reason (R): Nutrients in soil, such as nitrogen and potassium, come from the slow breakdown of rocks and the remains of plants and animals.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. The geosphere is the solid part of the Earth, including rocks, soils and minerals, so soil is part of it. R is a correct statement from the chapter about where soil nutrients come from.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Village X, on the coast of Karnataka, gets very heavy rain every year; Village Y, in western Rajasthan, gets very little. Which prediction does the chapter support?
questions.a: The kinds of plants and animals in X and Y are likely to differ The chapter says rainfall affects the kinds of plants and animals that can live in a place. Both villages have a hydrosphere and a geosphere.
o: The kinds of plants and animals in X and Y are likely to differ
X and Y will have the same plants, since all plants need the same soil
Only their groundwater will differ; rain does not affect living things
Y will have more kinds of animals, since less rain means fewer floods

questions.q:
Follow some water on its journey in the Western Ghats and name what is happening at each stage.
(a) Water vapour in the air forms clouds and falls as rain. Name the two Earth systems the water moves between. (1)
(b) The rain soaks into the soil, and nutrients from the soil dissolve in it. Which property of water allows this, and which Earth system is the soil part of? (1)
(c) A teak tree's roots take up this water. What does the water do inside the tree? (1)
(d) In the leaves, the water is used with a gas from the air, in sunlight, to make food. Name the process, the gas used and the gas given out. (1)
(e) A deer nearby breathes in the gas given out. Explain how stages (a) to (d) and this breath show the four Earth systems working together. (1)
questions.a: (a) From the atmosphere (as vapour and clouds) to the hydrosphere (as rain and water on land). (b) Water is a good solvent; soil is part of the geosphere. (c) It transports nutrients from the soil to the leaves. (d) Photosynthesis; carbon dioxide is used and oxygen is given out. (e) Water from the atmosphere and hydrosphere carries geosphere nutrients into a living tree (biosphere), whose oxygen returns to the atmosphere for the deer to breathe: each system supplies the next.
s: Atmosphere to hydrosphere
Water is a good solvent; soil is geosphere
Transports nutrients from soil to leaves
Photosynthesis, carbon dioxide in, oxygen out
Explains the chain as all four systems supporting one another

questions.q:
A bee visits one mustard flower and then another, carrying yellow pollen on its legs.
(a) Name the step the bee is carrying out, and say which gamete the pollen contains.
(b) What must happen after (a) for a seed to form? Name the cell formed and what it becomes.
questions.a: (a) Pollination; pollen grains are the male gametes. (b) Fertilisation: the male gamete from the pollen must combine with the female gamete in the ovule, deep inside the flower. This forms a zygote, which becomes the seed.
s: Pollination; pollen holds the male gametes
Fertilisation with the ovule forms a zygote, which becomes the seed

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Hydra grows small buds on its body that break off and grow into new individuals.
Statement 2: Planaria needs two parents in order to regrow from a fragment of its body.
Statement 3: A banyan seedling that grew from a seed dropped by a bird is an example of vegetative propagation.
Which statement(s) is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only. Statement 2 is wrong: Planaria regrows from a fragment of one body, which is asexual. Statement 3 is wrong: a seed forms by fertilisation, which is sexual reproduction; vegetative propagation is growing a new plant from a leaf, stem or root.
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
A peepal seedling is found growing out of a crack in a rooftop water tank in Varanasi, far from any peepal tree.
(a) Explain how the seed most probably got there.
(b) What allowed the seed to start growing in a crack with almost no soil?
(c) How does this way of spreading help the peepal plant?
questions.a: (a) A bird ate a peepal fruit and later dropped or excreted the seed on the tank, far from the parent tree. (b) The seed got water (from rain or the tank) and used its own stored nutrients to grow roots and shoots. (c) Seeds dropped far from the parent plant let the plant spread to new places.
s: A bird ate the fruit and dropped the seed far away
Water plus the seed's stored nutrients start roots and shoots
Helps the plant spread to new places

questions.q: Riya plants a stem cutting from her grandmother's money plant. Her friend sows seeds taken from a pumpkin that formed after insects carried pollen between pumpkin flowers. Which statement about the new plants is correct?
questions.a: The money plant copies its parent's instructions exactly; the pumpkin seedlings may vary The cutting is vegetative propagation, asexual, so it is an exact copy in instructions. The seeds come from sexual reproduction, where instructions from two parents mix, so the seedlings can differ.
o: The money plant copies its parent's instructions exactly; the pumpkin seedlings may vary
Both the money plant and the pumpkin seedlings will be exact copies of their parents
The pumpkin seedlings will be exact copies, while the money plant may vary from its parent
Neither will resemble its parent, since new plants get completely new instructions each time

questions.q:
Justify the chapter's statement: 'Reproduction does more than just create more of the same kind of living beings.'
(a) First, what would happen to life on Earth without reproduction, and what makes a calf grow into a cow? (1)
(b) Give two examples from the chapter of small changes passed down that helped living things survive. (2)
(c) Explain how sexual reproduction produces such differences. (1)
(d) What can such small differences lead to over many generations? (1)
questions.a: (a) Life would eventually disappear; genes, the instructions passed from parents and stored in every cell, make a calf grow into a cow. (b) Camels developing humps to store fat and survive in deserts; some bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics. (c) Each parent's gametes carry half its instructions, a different set each time, and they mix when gametes join, so offspring are not exactly like either parent. (d) They can add up to big differences, new features, or even completely new types of living beings.
s: Without reproduction life would disappear; genes make a calf grow into a cow
Camel humps
Antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Mixing of instructions from two gametes gives variation
Over generations: new features or new types of living beings

questions.q:
(a) In a laboratory, two mating types of yeast are mixed together and new yeast cells form. Which kind of reproduction is this, and will the new cells be identical to either parent?
(b) A Planaria is accidentally cut into three pieces, and each piece grows into a whole worm. Which kind of reproduction is this, and how will the three worms compare with the original one?
questions.a: (a) Sexual reproduction: the two mating types act like two parents, so their instructions combine and the new cells are not exactly like either parent. (b) Asexual reproduction (regrowing from a fragment): there is one parent, so all three worms are exact copies of the original in their instructions.
s: Yeast: sexual; offspring not identical to either parent
Planaria: asexual from fragments; exact copies of the one parent

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Camels have humps that store fat and help them survive in deserts.
Reason (R): Each camel grows a hump during its own lifetime because it has to live in the desert.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The chapter says camels developed humps over time, through small changes in the instructions passed down from parents to offspring over many generations, not by each camel growing one because it needs it.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A brother and a sister born to the same parents usually do not look exactly alike.
Reason (R): Each gamete carries a different set of instructions, and the instructions from the two parents mix in a different way each time.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Because each gamete carries a different set of instructions and they mix differently each time sperm and egg join, each child gets a unique mix, so siblings differ.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A sugarcane farmer in Mandya plants short pieces of cane stem in moist furrows, and new plants come up from them. He says he has never seen sugarcane seeds. Which conclusion fits the chapter best?
questions.a: The new plants grow from the stem pieces by vegetative propagation New plants growing from a planted part such as a stem is vegetative propagation, a form of asexual reproduction; no seed is needed.
o: The new plants grow from the stem pieces by vegetative propagation
Seeds must be hidden in the stem pieces, since plants only grow from seed
Each stem piece needs pollen from another plant before it can grow
The plants come from gametes of two parents joined inside the stem

questions.q:
A nursery owner in Pune has one rose plant whose flowers are an unusual deep red that customers love. She can raise new plants in two ways.
Plan 1: plant stem cuttings from this rose in moist soil.
Plan 2: sow the seeds that form after insects carry pollen to its flowers from other rose plants in the nursery.
(a) Which plan is vegetative propagation?
(b) In Plan 2, which two gametes join, and where in the flowers is each made?
(c) Explain why the seedlings from Plan 2 may not all have deep red flowers.
(d) Her aim is to sell more roses of exactly this deep red. Which plan should she use? Also give one advantage, from the chapter, of the variation that the other plan produces.
questions.a: (a) Plan 1. (b) The male gamete in pollen grains, made in the anther of another rose plant's flower, joins the female gamete in the ovule, found deep inside the deep red rose's flower. (c) The seedlings get mixed instructions from two parents, the deep red rose and the other rose, so they share some traits with each but are not exactly like either; flower colour can differ. (d) Plan 1: cuttings are asexual, so each new plant is an exact copy of the deep red rose in its instructions. Advantage of Plan 2's variation: small differences can help a plant survive better in a new environment, and new features can appear.
s: Plan 1 is vegetative propagation
Pollen from the anther joins the ovule inside the flower
Seedlings get mixed instructions from two parents, so colour may differ
Chooses Plan 1 (exact copies) and gives an advantage of variation

questions.q: Kunal claims: 'A child gets a complete set of instructions from the mother and another complete set from the father, so a child carries twice as many instructions as either parent.' Do you agree? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: No. Each parent makes gametes that carry only half of the parent's genetic material. When the male and female gametes join, the new cell has one complete set of instructions, half from each parent. If each gamete carried a full set, the amount would double in every generation, which does not happen.
s: Verdict: disagree
Gametes carry only half of each parent's genetic material
Joined cell has one complete set, half from each parent, so no doubling

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'A hen has to pack a large store of food into each egg she lays, but a cow does not need to store food in this way for her calf before it is born.'
questions.a: True. In birds, the embryo develops after the egg is laid, so the food in the egg has to last until it hatches. In most mammals, such as the cow, the embryo develops inside the mother's body, which supplies all the food and oxygen until birth.
s: States True
Bird embryo develops outside on stored food; mammal embryo is fed by the mother's body

questions.q: A frog lays her eggs on a dry rock several metres from a pond, and the male stays in the pond. Using the chapter's description of reproduction in frogs, show that these eggs cannot be fertilised and develop in the way the chapter describes.
questions.a: The chapter says male and female frogs eject sperm and eggs into the water, where they combine to form the zygote, and the zygote then develops into an embryo in the water. On a dry rock, far from the male's sperm in the pond, there is no water for the sperm to reach the eggs, so no zygote can form; and even a zygote would have no water to develop in.
s: Frog fertilisation happens when sperm and eggs combine in water
On dry rock the sperm cannot reach the eggs, so no zygote forms
The zygote also needs water to develop into an embryo

questions.q: Over several years, doctors at a hospital find that an antibiotic no longer kills some kinds of bacteria. Which idea from the chapter explains this?
