questions.a: Small changes in passed-on instructions helped some bacteria survive The chapter says reproduction allows small changes in instructions passed to offspring, and some bacteria have become resistant to antibiotics in this way, over generations.
o: Small changes in passed-on instructions helped some bacteria survive
Each bacterium learned to resist the drug after swallowing some of it
Bacteria always reproduce with two parents, so they never change at all
The antibiotic added brand-new instructions into the bacteria's cells

questions.q:
Compare reproduction in a frog, a sparrow and a goat.
(a) Where does fertilisation take place in each? (2)
(b) Where does the zygote develop into an embryo in each? (2)
(c) For the sparrow and the goat, explain how the developing embryo gets its food. (1)
questions.a: (a) Frog: outside the body, in water, where the male and female eject sperm and eggs. Sparrow and goat: inside the female's body, where sperm are deposited and swim to the egg. (b) Frog: in the water. Sparrow: outside the mother, after the egg is laid, during hatching. Goat: inside the mother's body. (c) Sparrow: from the food the mother stored in the egg, which must last until it hatches. Goat: from the mother's body, which supplies food and oxygen until birth.
s: Frog: external fertilisation in water
Sparrow and goat: internal fertilisation
Frog embryo develops in water
Sparrow embryo develops after laying; goat embryo inside the mother
Food: stored in the egg (sparrow) vs from the mother's body (goat)

questions.q:
Match each organism with the way it is described as reproducing.
Column A: 1. Amoeba  2. Hydra  3. Potato  4. Frog
Column B:
(a) New plants sprout from the 'eyes' when planted in moist soil.
(b) One cell splits into two identical individuals.
(c) A small outgrowth on the body breaks off and grows into a new individual.
(d) Sperm and eggs released into water combine there to form the zygote.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. Amoeba divides in two; Hydra reproduces by buds; potato 'eyes' show vegetative propagation; frogs have fertilisation in water.

questions.q: In an illustrative model, every cell of a parent holds 400 pages of instructions. If gametes carried the full 400 pages instead of half, the first offspring would hold 800 pages; going on the same way, the third generation of offspring would hold ___ pages.

Students at a farm school in Punjab mark three equal patches of a flowering mustard field (illustrative results).
Patch 1: left open to wind and insects; 80 pods formed per 100 flowers.
Patch 2: covered with a fine net that keeps insects out but lets wind through; 45 pods per 100 flowers.
Patch 3: each flower sealed in a paper bag that keeps out both wind and insects; 5 pods per 100 flowers.
(a) Which step of reproduction in plants is almost completely blocked in Patch 3? Explain why that means hardly any seeds form.
(b) How many fewer pods per 100 flowers does Patch 2 give than Patch 1, and what does this show about insects?
(c) Patch 2 still gives 45 pods per 100 flowers. Which carrier of pollen named in the chapter explains this?
(d) The farmer must spray against pests once. Spraying during flowering would kill the insects visiting the flowers; spraying just after flowering ends would let the pests destroy about 5 more pods per 100 flowers. When should he spray? Justify with the data.
questions.a: (a) Pollination: pollen cannot be carried to the flowers. Without pollen there is no fertilisation, so no zygote forms to become a seed. (b) 80 - 45 = 35 fewer pods per 100 flowers; insects carry a large share of the pollen. (c) Wind. (d) Just after flowering ends. Spraying during flowering would remove the insect carriers, which the nets show is worth about 35 pods per 100 flowers, while waiting costs only about 5 pods per 100 flowers to pests.
s: Pollination blocked, so no fertilisation, no zygote, no seed
35 fewer pods; insects carry much of the pollen
Wind
Spray after flowering: losing insects costs about 35 pods per 100 flowers, waiting about 5

questions.q:
A papaya is cut open, showing soft orange flesh and many black seeds.
(a) Which part of the flower developed into the flesh, and what formed each seed?
(b) Birds often eat papaya. Explain how this can help the papaya plant.
questions.a: (a) The fleshy part of the flower around the ovule developed into the fruit's flesh; each seed formed from a zygote made at fertilisation. (b) When birds eat the fruit, the seeds often get dropped far from the parent plant, which helps the plant spread to new places.
s: Flesh from the fleshy part around the ovule; seed from the zygote
Birds drop the seeds far away, spreading the plant

questions.q: Meena claims: 'In birds and in mammals, fertilisation takes place inside the female's body, so in both groups the embryo develops inside the mother until birth.' Check each part of her claim and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is correct: in birds and mammals, sperm are deposited inside the female's body and fertilisation happens there. The second part is wrong for birds: the fertilised egg is laid, and the zygote develops into an embryo after laying, during hatching, using food stored in the egg. Only in most mammals does the embryo develop inside the mother.
s: Accepts that fertilisation is internal in both
Corrects the bird case: egg laid, embryo develops outside on stored food
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
(a) What does the chapter compare genes to, and where in a living being are they stored?
(b) Some instructions guide the making of blood and others the forming of bones. Using (a), explain why a skin cell from a cow's ear still carries the instructions for making bones.
questions.a: (a) A detailed instruction manual; genes are stored inside every cell of a living being. (b) The chapter says the instructions are stored inside every cell, and that some guide the making of blood while others guide bones, muscles or skin. So a skin cell from the ear holds the instruction manual too, including the instructions for bones.
s: Instruction manual, stored in every cell
Instructions are in every cell, so the skin cell holds the bone instructions too

questions.q: Raghav says: 'Life on Earth is only at risk from huge disasters. Small changes in the air do not matter.' Which statement from the chapter goes against his view?
questions.a: A little less oxygen or a little less ozone could endanger life The chapter says even small changes in global temperature, oxygen levels or the ozone layer can put life at risk, because life depends on a delicate balance.
o: A little less oxygen or a little less ozone could endanger life
Life is safe as long as the total amount of air stays the same
Trees and plankton always balance out small changes straight away
Ozone matters only to plants, so small ozone changes spare people

questions.q:
A dye factory drains its waste into a river. Downstream, fish die, and farmers use the river water on their vegetable fields.
(a) Name two harms the chapter says such water pollution can cause.
(b) Explain how harmful substances from the factory can reach people who never drink the river water.
questions.a: (a) Any two: harm to aquatic life; water becomes unsafe; harmful substances spread through the food chain. (b) The polluted water is taken up by the crops (and the fish live in it); people who eat the vegetables or fish take in the harmful substances, which spread through the food chain.
s: Any two harms (aquatic life harmed, water unsafe, spread through food chain)
Explains spread to people through crops or fish in the food chain

questions.q:
A village panchayat in Kutch owns a large grassland where grasses feed deer and grasshoppers, and foxes hunt them. Two plans are offered (illustrative figures).
Plan A: plough 60 per cent of the grassland for cotton, using heavy doses of fertiliser; expected income Rs 9 lakh a year.
Plan B: plough 20 per cent, using sustainable farming practices and only the fertiliser the crop needs; expected income Rs 4 lakh a year.
(a) Which animals will lose their food first when the grass is ploughed?
(b) Explain how the foxes will be affected, even though nobody ploughs their dens.
(c) What does the chapter say excess fertilisers can do to soil, crops and the food chain?
(d) Plan A earns Rs 5 lakh more a year. Which plan should the panchayat choose? Justify using (a) to (c), and name one safeguard it should insist on.
questions.a: (a) The herbivores that feed on grasses: deer and grasshoppers. (b) Without herbivores, predators like foxes lose their food too, so they struggle as well. (c) Excess fertilisers pollute soil, reduce crop yield and spread harmful substances through the food chain. (d) Plan B. Plan A destroys three times as much habitat (60 per cent against 20 per cent), so more herbivores and then foxes would disappear, and its heavy fertiliser would pollute the soil, cut future yields and harm the food chain. The chapter says preserving biodiversity keeps ecosystems strong and balanced and that sustainable farming protects soil, so Plan B protects the land's balance even though it earns less. Safeguard: for example, the other 80 per cent of the grassland stays unploughed, or fertiliser is limited to what the crop needs.
s: Deer and grasshoppers (herbivores)
Foxes lose their prey, so they struggle too
Pollutes soil, reduces crop yield, spreads harm through the food chain
Chooses Plan B with reasons from (a) to (c) and names a safeguard

questions.q:
Match each international agreement with the result or detail the chapter gives for it.
Column A: 1. Montreal Protocol (1987)  2. Earth Summit (1992)  3. Kyoto Protocol (2005)  4. Paris Agreement (2015)
Column B:
(a) Because of it, the layer that blocks the Sun's UV rays is slowly recovering.
(b) It set a warming goal that, as of 2025, the world is not on track to meet.
(c) It started international efforts on both climate change and biodiversity.
(d) Dated 18 years after the CFC agreement, it committed countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
questions.a: 1-a, 2-c, 3-d, 4-b. Montreal cut CFCs so the ozone layer is recovering; the Earth Summit began efforts on climate and biodiversity; Kyoto (2005, 18 years after 1987) committed countries to cut emissions; Paris set the 1.5 degrees Celsius goal, which the world is not on track to meet.

questions.q:
Explain how burning fossil fuels leads to climate change.
(a) Name two greenhouse gases released when coal and oil are burnt. (1)
(b) What do these gases do in the atmosphere, and what is the result called? (1)
(c) Earth normally keeps a balance of carbon dioxide. Explain the balance and why burning fossil fuels upsets it. (1)
(d) Predict two effects of even a small rise in global temperature that would matter for a coastal town such as Puri, and explain each. (2)
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide and methane. (b) They trap even more heat in the atmosphere, causing global warming. (c) Trees, plants and tiny ocean plankton absorb carbon dioxide as they grow; burning fossil fuels releases extra carbon that was locked underground for millions of years, faster than Earth can absorb it, so heat builds up. (d) Any two, explained: ice caps melt and sea levels rise, which could flood the town; extreme weather conditions could strike the coast; plants and animals the town depends on, such as fish, could disappear.
s: Carbon dioxide and methane
They trap more heat, causing global warming
Plants and plankton absorb carbon dioxide, but fossil carbon is released too fast
First effect relevant to a coastal town, explained
Second, different effect

questions.q: A notice on a colony board says: 'If our colony plants a few trees, they will soak up all the carbon dioxide from the city's vehicles, so nobody needs to cut down on fuel.' Is the notice right? Use the chapter to justify your answer.
questions.a: No. Trees, plants and ocean plankton do absorb carbon dioxide, but burning fuels releases extra carbon, locked underground for millions of years, faster than Earth can absorb it, so heat still builds up. The chapter says protecting the climate means cutting greenhouse gases: using renewable energy, improving energy use and choosing environmentally friendly travel. Planting trees helps but cannot replace cutting fuel use.
s: Verdict: disagree
Extra carbon is released faster than plants can absorb it
Cutting emissions (renewables, better energy use, greener travel) is still needed

questions.q: A family's scooter burns 1 litre of petrol a day, and each litre releases about 2.3 kg of carbon dioxide (illustrative figure). If the family cycles instead on 3 days of a week, it avoids about ___ kg of carbon dioxide that week.

A city newspaper in one week reports: (i) a coastal road flooded as the sea rises higher than before; (ii) a patch of mangrove forest cut down, and the birds that lived there gone; (iii) thick smog over the city that sends people to hospital with breathing problems.
(a) Match each report to one part of the triple planetary crisis.
(b) Report (ii) can also add to the problem in report (i). Explain how, using what the chapter says about trees and carbon dioxide.
questions.a: (a) (i) Climate change (rising sea levels); (ii) biodiversity loss (habitat destroyed, animals gone); (iii) pollution (air pollution causing smog and breathing problems). (b) Trees and plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow. Cutting the mangroves removes some of this absorption, so more carbon dioxide stays in the air, trapping more heat; warming can melt ice caps and raise sea levels, as in report (i).
s: (i) climate change, (ii) biodiversity loss, (iii) pollution
Fewer trees absorb less carbon dioxide, adding to warming and rising seas

questions.q: A leader announces: 'If every country simply cuts its greenhouse gas emissions, the whole triple planetary crisis will be solved.' Using the chapter, show that this cannot be enough on its own.
questions.a: Cutting greenhouse gases tackles climate change. But the triple planetary crisis also includes biodiversity loss, caused when natural habitats are destroyed, and pollution, such as factory, farm and plastic waste in water and soil, and excess fertilisers. Cutting emissions does not stop habitats being destroyed or waste being dumped, so preserving biodiversity and better waste management and sustainable farming are also needed.
s: Cutting emissions mainly tackles climate change
Biodiversity loss comes from habitat destruction, which needs separate action
Pollution from waste and fertilisers needs waste management and sustainable farming

questions.q:
True or false? Give a reason.
'Climate change just means that some days of the year become a little hotter.'
questions.a: False. The chapter calls climate change the long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather patterns. Warming can melt ice caps, raise sea levels and flood coastal cities, cause extreme weather and lead to many plants and animals disappearing; it is far more than a few hotter days.
s: States False
Long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather, with wider effects such as rising seas or extreme weather

questions.q: Plan a five-point 'Protect Our Planet' week for your school. For each of the five points, write one action taken from the chapter's advice and name which part of the triple planetary crisis it helps to reduce. Use at least one action for each of the three parts.
questions.a: Sample: (1) Repair and swap-meet for old clothes and bags: reusing and repairing reduce pollution and waste. (2) Switch off fans and lights in empty rooms and fix leaking taps: saving energy and water reduces greenhouse gases and waste (climate change). (3) Walk or cycle to school day: environmentally friendly travel cuts greenhouse gases (climate change). (4) Protect the school's patch of trees and plant native shrubs: preserving habitats and biodiversity (biodiversity loss). (5) Separate plastic for recycling and stop burning leaves: less plastic waste and less air pollution (pollution).
s: Action 1 from the chapter, linked to a crisis part
Action 2, linked
Action 3, linked
Action 4, linked
Action 5, linked, with all three parts covered

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Even a small increase in global temperature can put many coastal cities at risk.
Reason (R): A rise in temperature can melt ice caps and raise sea levels.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says even a small increase in temperature can melt ice caps and raise sea levels, which could flood many coastal cities; that is exactly why coastal cities are at risk.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In a grassland, most of the grasses die out after the land is dug up for a quarry. Following the chapter's own example, what happens next?
questions.a: Deer and grasshoppers struggle first, and then the predators that eat them Herbivores that feed on grasses struggle to survive; without herbivores, predators like tigers or foxes lose their food too.
o: Deer and grasshoppers struggle first, and then the predators that eat them
Foxes and tigers struggle first, and the deer then have plenty of food
Only the grasses are affected, since animals can always find other food
The grasshoppers increase, because they no longer have grass to compete with

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur uses 1200 units of electricity a month, all from a coal power station. Illustrative figures: each unit from coal releases about 0.8 kg of carbon dioxide; a grown tree takes in about 20 kg of carbon dioxide a year. The school has funds for only one project: rooftop solar panels that would supply 750 units a month, or planting trees on its spare land, which has room for about 40 trees.
(a) Which part of the triple planetary crisis does the school's coal electricity add to, and why?
(b) How much carbon dioxide would the solar panels avoid in a month, and in a year?
(c) How many grown trees would be needed to take in the same amount in a year as the solar panels avoid? How much do the 40 trees take in?
(d) Which project should the school fund? Justify using (b), (c) and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Climate change: burning coal releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps more heat and causes global warming. (b) 750 x 0.8 = 600 kg a month; 600 x 12 = 7200 kg a year. (c) 7200 / 20 = 360 trees; 40 trees take in 40 x 20 = 800 kg a year. (d) The solar panels. questions.q: Differentiate between global warming and climate change, as the chapter uses the two terms, and say how they are connected.
questions.a: Global warming is what the chapter calls the result when greenhouse gases trap even more heat in the atmosphere. Climate change is the long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather patterns. The extra trapped heat (global warming) leads to climate change.
s: Global warming: extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases; climate change: long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather
Connection: warming causes the climate changes

questions.q: Write a short situation set in or near your own town in which all three parts of the triple planetary crisis appear and are linked to each other. Then name each part and point to where it appears in your situation.
questions.a: Sample: A river town clears a wetland to build a truck depot. The birds and fish of the wetland disappear (biodiversity loss). Diesel trucks at the depot fill the air with smoke, causing breathing problems (pollution), and the fuel they burn releases carbon dioxide that adds to global warming and the long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather that it brings (climate change). The three are linked because one decision caused all of them.
s: A believable local situation
Biodiversity loss, pollution and climate change each clearly present and named
Shows how the three are linked (one cause or one leading to another)

questions.q: Trees, plants and tiny ocean plankton absorb carbon dioxide as they grow. Why, then, does burning coal and oil still make heat build up in the atmosphere?
questions.a: It releases carbon locked underground faster than Earth can absorb it Burning fossil fuels releases extra carbon that was locked underground for millions of years, and Earth cannot absorb it fast enough, so heat builds up.
o: It releases carbon locked underground faster than Earth can absorb it
Burning coal stops trees and plankton from taking in any carbon dioxide
Coal smoke is made of CFCs, which trap heat inside the ozone layer itself
Carbon dioxide from coal is a different gas from the one that trees take in

questions.q:
A school replaces its diesel generator with solar panels and starts a weekly 'cycle to school' day.
(a) Which part of the triple planetary crisis do these steps mainly reduce, and how?
(b) The chapter says preserving biodiversity is also key. Give the chapter's reason, and say why the school's two steps alone do not do this.
questions.a: (a) Climate change: solar energy (renewable) and cycling (environmentally friendly travel) burn less fuel, so fewer greenhouse gases are released. (b) Diverse ecosystems are stronger and more balanced. The two steps cut emissions but do not protect habitats or living things directly.
s: Climate change, by burning less fuel and releasing fewer greenhouse gases
Diverse ecosystems are stronger and more balanced; the steps do not protect habitats

questions.q:
Compare the Montreal Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
(a) For each, state the year and the problem it set out to tackle. (2)
(b) Which part of Earth's atmosphere did the Montreal Protocol help protect, and why does that part matter for life? (1)
(c) What does the chapter say about the progress of each agreement? (1)
(d) Using (c), judge whether the chapter shows that global agreements are enough on their own. (1)
questions.a: (a) Montreal Protocol, 1987: harmful chemicals called CFCs. Paris Agreement, 2015: greenhouse gas emissions, with a goal of limiting warming to below 1.5 degrees Celsius. (b) The ozone layer, which blocks harmful UV rays from the Sun that can damage living cells. (c) After Montreal, CFCs were reduced and the ozone layer is slowly recovering. For Paris, as of 2025 the world is not on track to meet the 1.5 degree goal. (d) Not on their own. One agreement worked, but the other is off track; the chapter says much more action is needed, from local communities to global leaders, including everyday actions.
s: Montreal 1987, CFCs
Paris 2015, greenhouse gases and the 1.5 degree goal
Ozone layer, which blocks UV harmful to living cells
Montreal: ozone recovering; Paris: not on track as of 2025
Judgement: agreements help but more action by everyone is needed

questions.q: A family in Bhubaneswar wants to follow the chapter's advice on cutting pollution and waste at home. Which action fits that advice?
questions.a: Getting a torn school bag stitched instead of buying a new one The chapter says reusing, repairing and recycling items like clothes and plastic reduce pollution and waste. Burning plastic pollutes the air, one tree cannot make up for fuel burnt, and excess fertiliser pollutes the soil.
o: Getting a torn school bag stitched instead of buying a new one
Burning old plastic bags at home so that they never reach a landfill
Planting one tree so the family can keep driving its car on short trips
Using extra fertiliser in the kitchen garden to grow bigger vegetables
